title: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (7 of 7)
hook: a mongoose, half gold, rolls through a king's great sacrifice and says it isn't enough
tomorrow: Bhakti yoga: the nine forms of devotion; the Alvars and Nayanars; Mirabai, Tulsidas, Surdas; kirtan as method (1 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ghost and the dog's curly tail. We help ourselves, not the world; work like a master, not a slave. Today, the last day of karma yoga.
screen: `THE WORLD IS A DOG'S CURLY TAIL.`

segments.voice: The great war of the Mahabharata is over. The winner, King Yudhishthira, holds an enormous sacrifice to mark his reign: gold for the priests, food for the crowds, gifts on every side. Then, in the middle of the ceremony, a mongoose runs in. Half its body is ordinary brown fur. The other half shines like gold. It rolls on the ground, gets up, looks at itself, and says: this great sacrifice isn't equal to a little barley flour once given by a poor family. Everyone goes quiet. What family? What flour?
screen: `A KING'S GREAT SACRIFICE.` → `A MONGOOSE, HALF GOLD.` → `NOT EQUAL TO A LITTLE FLOUR.`

segments.voice: The mongoose tells them. There was a famine. A poor brahmin lived with his wife, his son and his son's wife, and for days they'd had nothing. At last they got a little barley flour, just enough for four small portions. They were about to eat when a guest came to the door, starving. The father gave his portion. The guest was still hungry. The wife gave hers. Then the son. Then the daughter-in-law. The guest ate, and revealed himself: he was Dharma, the god of righteousness himself, and he blessed them. The mongoose had come out of its hole and rolled in the few grains left on the floor, and wherever the flour touched, it turned to gold. Ever since, it's gone from sacrifice to sacrifice, rolling on the ground, looking for another gift that great, to turn the other half gold. It still hasn't found one. Vivekananda retold this story in his talks on karma yoga. The point isn't that kings shouldn't give. It's that an offering's size isn't measured by its price. It's measured by what it costs the one who gives it, and by how freely it's given. That's where the week has been going. Each is great in its own place, like the birds. Duty done with care, like the woman and the butcher. Your own work as worship. The work changing the worker. And now: the smallest gift, fully given, outweighing gold.
screen: `FOUR PORTIONS OF BARLEY FLOUR.` · `EACH ONE GIVEN TO A GUEST.` · `THE GRAINS THAT TURNED TO GOLD.` · `MEASURED BY WHAT IT COSTS.` · then, large: `OFFER THE WORK.`

segments.voice: Look back over the week and let each picture pass with a breath: the birds and their fire, the woman at the door, the butcher feeding his parents, the first roti, the curly tail, the mongoose. Then ask: what's one small thing I gave this week that nobody saw? Don't grade it, just notice it was given; if you pray, offer the whole week as it was, and if not, rest in it.
Saktu, barley flour, the poor family's whole gift. The path of action, offered: your own work, in your own place, done with care, given freely. Small gifts can outweigh gold.
Your line: offer the work. Tomorrow, a new road: devotion. That's the karma week, finished.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often retell the Mahabharata's story of the half-golden mongoose to explain that the worth of a gift, a sacrifice or a day's work lies in how freely and fully it's given, not in its size.

chat.says: Why did the mongoose say a little flour beat the king's huge sacrifice?
options: Because the poor family gave all they had, freely, though it cost them a lot.
Because the king's gifts had secretly been taken from the poor.
Because barley flour was worth more than gold in those days.
